opus-5.5.text:
I think the interesting thing about ARC is that every task is, in principle, solvable from a handful of examples. The rule is always there in the grids. So when a human gets stuck, it's usually not because the information is missing. It's because the search over possible explanations went down the wrong path.

When you look at a task, you immediately bring a bunch of priors: objectness, symmetry, counting, gravity, containment, things being "the same kind" because they share a color. Most of the time those priors are a gift. They're why people can solve a task in thirty seconds that a brute-force program search would struggle with. But they also mean you commit early to a framing. If you decide the task is about color, and it's actually about the topology of the shapes, you can stare at it for ten minutes and keep refining the wrong hypothesis. You tweak details instead of throwing the frame away.

A second failure mode is compositional depth. Individually, the transformations are often simple: reflect this, recolor that, extend a line until it hits something. But when a task chains three or four of these, and the examples only partly reveal each step, your working memory becomes the bottleneck. You can see two of the pieces but not hold them all together and check them against every example at once.

Third, some tasks use a concept that's salient to the designer but not to you. The prior just isn't activated. Once someone points it out, you get the "aha" and it feels obvious in hindsight. That's quite telling. It suggests the difficulty is in hypothesis generation, not verification. Checking a proposed rule is easy. Producing the right candidate is hard.

That's also why I find ARC useful for thinking about AI systems, including the evolutionary and LLM-driven program search work we've been doing. You can look at where models fail versus where humans fail, and they're often different places. Humans fail on long compositional chains or misleading surface features. Models historically failed on the really basic perceptual priors humans get for free. The interesting research question is how you build a system that keeps the human-like priors for proposing hypotheses, but also has the patience to discard a framing and search more broadly when the first idea doesn't fit.

r001.rationale: The response explains that a solver’s priors and framing affect which rule they notice: a useful framing can make a task quick to solve, while a misleading one can obscure the solution.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think that's actually one of the most interesting questions about ARC, because the whole premise of the benchmark, going back to Chollet's original framing, is that these tasks should be easy for humans. They're built on core knowledge priors: objectness, basic geometry, counting, symmetry, that sort of thing. So when a human gets stuck, it tells you something about where the difficulty actually lives, and it's usually not in the primitives themselves.

What I've seen, both from looking at the human performance data and honestly from sitting down and trying to solve these myself, is that failures tend to fall into a few buckets. The first is just search. A lot of ARC tasks compose three, four, five primitive operations, and even if each one is trivial, the space of compositions grows very fast. A human looks at the demonstration pairs, forms a hypothesis, tests it against the examples, and if it doesn't fit, they have to backtrack. People are not great at systematic backtracking. You get anchored on your first hypothesis, you keep trying to patch it instead of throwing it away.

The second bucket is perceptual. Some tasks have grids that are large or noisy, and the relevant structure is a small object or a subtle relationship, maybe the count of something, or which object is the odd one out. If you parse the grid the wrong way, if you chunk it into the wrong objects, you'll never find the rule, because the rule is stated in terms of a decomposition you didn't make. I think this is underappreciated. We talk about ARC as a reasoning benchmark, but a lot of it is really about getting the right representation first.

And the third thing is ambiguity. With only two or three demonstration pairs, there are often multiple rules consistent with the examples, and the intended one is whatever the task designer had in mind. So the human has to do a kind of Bayesian inference over the designer's intent, and sometimes the simpler rule in your head isn't the one that was meant. The puzzles that trip people up the most are often the ones where the rule is simple but surprising, where there's a cheaper explanation that happens to also fit the training pairs.

So I'd say the honest answer is that humans fail for reasons that are actually quite similar in kind to why models fail, just at a different scale. It's program synthesis under a tight budget, with a noisy perceptual front end and a limited ability to keep multiple hypotheses alive at once. What's different is how humans recover: they can step back, re-segment the grid, reconsider what the objects are. And that flexibility in representation, that's really the thing we're trying to get into these systems.

r001.rationale: The response explains that a solver’s representation and perspective affect whether they find the rule: a wrong object decomposition can hide it, while re-segmenting the grid can help reveal it.

astra-6.text:
I think you have to distinguish between not seeing the rule and not being able to execute it. You can stare at an ARC task and think, “I have absolutely no idea what’s going on,” and then somebody gives you a tiny hint—perhaps you should look at the empty space rather than the colored objects—and suddenly it becomes obvious. Your ability to reason hasn’t changed. What’s changed is the representation you’re using.

You’re trying to infer a program from very few examples, and there are many possible explanations. Humans bring priors about objects, symmetry, counting, and so on. Those make the search manageable, but they can also lead you down the wrong path. You latch onto an interpretation and keep trying to make it work.

So when a task stumps a human, I’d want to know where that process broke down. Did they miss a relevant feature? Did they get stuck on the wrong abstraction? Or did they understand the transformation but struggle to apply it consistently? The final answer alone doesn’t really tell you that.

r001.rationale: The response says a hint can change the solver’s representation and make the solution suddenly obvious, identifying perspective as a factor.

sol-6.1.text:
I think you have to distinguish between finding the rule and executing the rule. You can look at an ARC task and, once someone explains it, say, “Oh, that’s obvious.” But that doesn’t mean it was obvious which hypothesis you should consider in the first place.

You’re given a few input-output examples, and there are many possible explanations. You might interpret something as an object that should move, when actually you need to count its parts or recognize a symmetry. Once you commit to one interpretation, it can be quite difficult to step back and change that representation.

So when a task stumps a human, I wouldn’t immediately conclude that it requires some extraordinarily sophisticated reasoning. It might require a very simple operation that the person just doesn’t think to try. That search over possible interpretations is a big part of the difficulty.

r001.rationale: The response explains that a solver’s choice of interpretation or hypothesis affects whether the solution seems obvious, even when the underlying operation is simple.
